derivations.claim: Write $e=(e_x,e_y,e_z)$. Substituting the stated diagonal tensor and $k=(k_x,0,k_z)$ into [L1], and expanding the cross products componentwise, gives $\begin{pmatrix}\omega^2\varepsilon_\perp-k_z^2/\mu&0&k_xk_z/\mu\\0&\omega^2\varepsilon_\perp-(k_x^2+k_z^2)/\mu&0\\k_xk_z/\mu&0&\omega^2\varepsilon_\parallel-k_x^2/\mu\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix}e_x\\e_y\\e_z\end{pmatrix}=0$.

If $e_y\ne0$, the middle row gives $k_x^2+k_z^2=\mu\varepsilon_\perp\omega^2$. If $(e_x,e_z)\ne(0,0)$, the $xz$ block must be singular, and its determinant is $\frac{\omega^2\varepsilon_\perp\varepsilon_\parallel}{\mu}\left(\mu\omega^2-\frac{k_x^2}{\varepsilon_\parallel}-\frac{k_z^2}{\varepsilon_\perp}\right)$, so it vanishes exactly on the second sheet. Conversely, on the first sheet $(0,1,0)$ is a nonzero kernel vector, and on the second sheet the singular $xz$ block has a nonzero kernel vector. Since the matrix separates the $y$ and $xz$ sectors, these are all nonzero modes.

At an intersection with $\varepsilon_\perp\ne\varepsilon_\parallel$, dividing the first sheet by $\varepsilon_\perp$ and subtracting the second gives $k_x^2(1/\varepsilon_\perp-1/\varepsilon_\parallel)=0$, hence $k_x=0$; either sheet then gives $k_z^2=\mu\varepsilon_\perp\omega^2$. Conversely, substituting these values into both sheets verifies an intersection. The matrix in step 1.1 is then $\operatorname{diag}(0,0,\omega^2\varepsilon_\parallel)$, so its kernel is the complex span of $\hat x,\hat y$. For $\varepsilon_\perp=\varepsilon_\parallel=\varepsilon$, take any real $k\in\mathbb R^3\setminus\{0\}$. Expanding the cross products in [L1] gives $\mathcal M(k,\omega)=(\varepsilon\omega^2-|k|^2/\mu)I_3+kk^T/\mu$. Every complex amplitude has the direct decomposition $e=e_\parallel+e_\perp$, where $e_\parallel=k(k\cdot e)/|k|^2$ and $k\cdot e_\perp=0$; the denominator is positive since $k$ is real and nonzero. The symbol acts by $\mathcal M e_\parallel=\varepsilon\omega^2e_\parallel$ and $\mathcal M e_\perp=(\varepsilon\omega^2-|k|^2/\mu)e_\perp$. Because $\varepsilon\omega^2>0$, a nonzero kernel occurs exactly on $|k|^2=\mu\varepsilon\omega^2$, and there it is precisely $k^\perp=\{e:k\cdot e=0\}$. This complex space has dimension two: choose an index with $k_i\ne0$ and solve its one linear equation for $e_i$ in terms of the other two complex coordinates. For every real unit direction $n$, taking $k=\omega\sqrt{\mu\varepsilon}\,n$ gives a point on that sphere. In the $xz$ section this kernel is the sum of the $y$ and transverse $xz$ coordinate sectors, verifying the common-circle section as well as the full-sphere claim. This proves the stated degeneracies and completes the conditional model classification.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. For $n\ge2$, a bounded $C^1$ domain Omega and $F\in C^1(\overline\Omega;\mathbb R^n)$, $\int_\Omega\operatorname{div}F\,dx=\int_{\partial\Omega}F\cdot\nu\,dS$.

This definition calls the coefficient model **reciprocal** when $\varepsilon(x)^T=\varepsilon(x)$ and $\mu(x)^T=\mu(x)$ at every $x\in\overline\Omega$. It places no Hermitian, positive-definite, or passivity condition on these complex matrices.
A nonzero amplitude $e$ is a source-free plane-wave mode in this branch exactly when $\mathcal M(k,\omega)e=0$; its magnetic amplitudes are $b=(k\times e)/\omega$ and $h=b/\mu$.

derivations.claim: Put $X=E_1\times H_2-E_2\times H_1$. For the first product write $E_1=U+iV$ and $H_2=W+iZ$ with real C1 fields. The complex-bilinear product is $E_1\times H_2=(U\times W-V\times Z)+i(U\times Z+V\times W)$; applying [F1] to each real pair and using the componentwise real-linearity of curl and divergence gives $\operatorname{div}(E_1\times H_2)=H_2\cdot\operatorname{curl}E_1-E_1\cdot\operatorname{curl}H_2$. The same expansion for $E_2\times H_1$ yields $\operatorname{div}X=H_2\cdot\operatorname{curl}E_1-E_1\cdot\operatorname{curl}H_2-H_1\cdot\operatorname{curl}E_2+E_2\cdot\operatorname{curl}H_1$. Substituting [L1] yields $E_2\cdot J_1-E_1\cdot J_2+i\omega(H_2\cdot\mu H_1-H_1\cdot\mu H_2+E_1\cdot\varepsilon E_2-E_2\cdot\varepsilon E_1)$. For any complex vectors $u,v$, $u\cdot\varepsilon v=\sum_{r,s}u_r\varepsilon_{rs}v_s=v\cdot\varepsilon u$ by swapping $r,s$ and using $\varepsilon_{rs}=\varepsilon_{sr}$; the same calculation applies to $\mu$. Thus the tensor terms cancel without conjugation and $\operatorname{div}X=E_2\cdot J_1-E_1\cdot J_2$.

The field $X$ is C1 on $\overline\Omega$. Apply [F2] separately to its real and imaginary parts, which satisfy the theorem's real-valued hypotheses, and combine the two identities complex-linearly. Substituting step 1.1 into the resulting equality gives the displayed boundary identity.

By [L2], the lossless anisotropic plane-wave branch has a real symmetric tensor $\varepsilon$ and scalar $\mu$; therefore its ordinary transposes equal themselves, so it is a subcase of the coefficient class in [L1]. Applying step 2.1 to any two C1 phasor solutions in that subcase proves the final sentence of the Statement.

If either solution pair is zero, every term in step 1.1 and in the boundary identity vanishes by bilinearity.
The scalar isotropic subcase is included in step 3.1 because scalar multiples of the identity are transpose-symmetric.
Step 1.1 uses only pointwise transpose symmetry and no inverse or positive eigenvalue, so singular symmetric coefficients are allowed.
At omega=0 the frequency-multiplied tensor terms in step 1.1 vanish; step 2.1 remains the static divergence identity.
Statement assumes AC_omega; step 2.1 applies the divergence theorem separately to the real and imaginary parts under that premise. No additional family of witnesses is selected.

The item does not infer tensor symmetry from the boundary identity; it proves only the stated sufficient condition.

derivations.claim: Since $\varepsilon_\perp,\varepsilon_\parallel>0$, the diagonal matrix $\varepsilon$ is invertible, so $e=\varepsilon^{-1}d=d_0(k_z/\varepsilon_\perp,0,-k_x/\varepsilon_\parallel)$ is defined and nonzero. Direct contraction gives $k\cdot d=d_0(k_xk_z-k_zk_x)=0$ and $k\cdot e=d_0k_xk_z(1/\varepsilon_\perp-1/\varepsilon_\parallel)\ne0$ by the nonzero-component and unequal-permittivity hypotheses.

The extraordinary dispersion relation gives $k_x^2/\varepsilon_\parallel+k_z^2/\varepsilon_\perp=\mu\omega^2$. Hence the $x$ and $z$ components of $k\times(k\times e)$ are $-d_0k_z(k_x^2/\varepsilon_\parallel+k_z^2/\varepsilon_\perp)=-\mu\omega^2d_0k_z$ and $d_0k_x(k_x^2/\varepsilon_\parallel+k_z^2/\varepsilon_\perp)=\mu\omega^2d_0k_x$, while the $y$ component is zero. Thus $\mu^{-1}k\times(k\times e)+\omega^2d=0$, so $e$ is an extraordinary symbol mode and the longitudinal-component claim follows.

derivations.claim: The denominator $(\omega_0^2-\omega^2)^2+\gamma^2\omega^2$ is strictly positive because $\gamma\omega>0$. Therefore [F1] gives $\operatorname{Im}\varepsilon(\omega)=a\gamma\omega/((\omega_0^2-\omega^2)^2+\gamma^2\omega^2)>0$. A scalar multiple of $I_3$ equals its ordinary transpose even when the scalar is complex, and the real scalar $\mu$ also equals its transpose; hence [F2] places these coefficients in the reciprocal class. The reciprocity identity [L1] is consequently applicable whenever the corresponding C1 phasor solutions exist.

By [F1], $P_1(t)=\operatorname{Re}(p_1e^{-i\omega t})$ has amplitude $p_1=(\varepsilon-\varepsilon_\infty)e$, so $J_{\mathrm{osc}}=\partial_tP_1$ has phasor amplitude $j_{\mathrm{osc}}=-i\omega p_1$. For any complex scalar amplitudes $u,v$, write the product as $\frac14(uv e^{-2i\omega t}+uv^*+u^*v+u^*v^*e^{2i\omega t})$. The period integrals of $e^{\pm2i\omega t}$ are zero because $\omega>0$, so the average is $\frac12\operatorname{Re}(uv^*)$. Applying this componentwise gives $\overline q_{\mathrm{osc}}=\frac12\operatorname{Re}(j_{\mathrm{osc}}\cdot e^*)=\frac{\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}(\varepsilon-\varepsilon_\infty)|e|^2=\frac{\omega}{2}\operatorname{Im}\varepsilon|e|^2>0$, since $\varepsilon_\infty$ is real and $e\ne0$. Positive $\overline q_{\mathrm{osc}}$ is work transferred from the field to the oscillator-current contribution in the adopted Maxwell sign convention. This is a model deduction, not an observation.
